hmmt-nov-2009-team-01.title: Area and semiperimeter
hmmt-nov-2009-team-01.body:
The legs have length $\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13$. The area of $T$ is $\frac12\cdot10\cdot12=60$ and the semiperimeter is $\frac{13+13+10}2=18$, so the inradius is $\frac{60}{18}=\frac{10}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{10}3$**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-02.title: Similar configuration
hmmt-nov-2009-team-02.body:
Let the apex half-angle be $\theta$; the legs are $13$, the half-base is $5$, so $\sin\theta=\frac5{13}$. A circle of radius $r$ tangent to both legs has its centre on the axis at distance $d=r/\sin\theta$ from the apex. For consecutive circles, $d_i-d_{i+1}=r_i+r_{i+1}$, i.e. $\frac{r_i-r_{i+1}}{\sin\theta}=r_i+r_{i+1}$, so $13(r_i-r_{i+1})=5(r_i+r_{i+1})$, giving $8r_i=18r_{i+1}$ and $\frac{r_{i+1}}{r_i}=\frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac49$**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-03.title: Geometric series
hmmt-nov-2009-team-03.body:
The radii form a geometric sequence with first term $\frac{10}3$ and ratio $\frac49$, so the areas $\pi r_i^2$ form a geometric sequence with first term $\frac{100\pi}9$ and ratio $\frac{16}{81}$. The sum is $\frac{100\pi}{9}\cdot\frac{1}{1-16/81}=\frac{100\pi}9\cdot\frac{81}{65}=\frac{180\pi}{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac{180\pi}{13}$**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-04.title: Pythagoras
hmmt-nov-2009-team-04.body:
The ball travels $7$ horizontally and $h$ vertically, so $h^2+7^2=53$, $h=2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-05.title: Unfold the rectangle
hmmt-nov-2009-team-05.body:
Reflect the rectangle across the sides instead of reflecting the path: the ball moves along a straight line with direction $(7,2)$. Between consecutive bounces off the left/right sides it climbs $2$ units for every $7$ units across. The path reaches a corner of some copy when both $7a$ and $2a$ are multiples of $7$ and $12$: smallest $a=6$, at $(42,12)$. Before that it crosses the vertical lines $x=7,14,21,28,35$ (five bounces) and no horizontal line (it reaches height $12$ only at the end, in the corner). So there are $5$ bounces.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-06.title: Pythagoras with the altitude
hmmt-nov-2009-team-06.body:
Let the triangle be $ABC$ with launch vertex $A$, hit point $Y$ on $BC$, and $M$ the midpoint of $BC$. Then $AM=\frac{5\sqrt3}2$ and $AM\perp BC$, so $MY^2=19-\frac{75}4=\frac14$, $MY=\frac12$. Thus $BY=\frac52-\frac12=2$ (and $CY=3$), so the nearest vertex is at distance $2$.

**Answer: 2**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-07.title: Unfold the triangle
hmmt-nov-2009-team-07.body:
Instead of reflecting the path, reflect the triangle across the side the ball hits, repeatedly; the ball then travels along a straight line. Put the launch vertex $A$ at the origin, $B=(5,0)$ and $C=\left(\frac52,\frac{5\sqrt3}2\right)$; the first hit is $Y=\left(\frac72,\frac{3\sqrt3}2\right)$ on $BC$ (at distance $2$ from $C$), and $AY=\sqrt{19}$. The line $AY$ has slope $\frac{3\sqrt3}{7}$. It first passes through a vertex of the triangular grid at $\left(\frac{35}2,\frac{15\sqrt3}2\right)=2(5,0)+3\left(\frac52,\frac{5\sqrt3}2\right)$. On the way it crosses $2$ horizontal grid lines, $1$ upward-sloping line and $4$ downward-sloping lines, i.e. $7$ walls. So the ball bounces $7$ times.

**Answer: 7**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-08.title: Unfold and count lattice points
hmmt-nov-2009-team-08.body:
Unfold the triangle by repeated reflection to tile the plane. Every vertex of the tiling, with the launch vertex at the origin, can be written uniquely as $a(5,0)+b\left(\frac52,\frac{5\sqrt3}2\right)$ with non-negative integers $a,b$ (for launch directions inside the triangle's angle). A straight ray to this vertex crosses $2(a+b)-3$ grid lines, i.e. the ball bounces $2(a+b)-3$ times. For $2009$ bounces we need $a+b=1006$.

The ray reaches the vertex for the *first* time only if no earlier vertex lies on it, i.e. $\gcd(a,b)=1$, i.e. $\gcd(a,1006)=1$. Since $1006=2\cdot503$, $a$ must be odd and not $503$. Among $a=1,\dots,1005$ this leaves $\varphi(1006)=502$ values. Each gives a different direction, so there are $502$ ways.

**Answer: 502**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-09.title: Expected values
hmmt-nov-2009-team-09.body:
Let $E_i$ be the expected number of further doors from room $i$, with $E_3=0$. Then $E_i=1+\frac34E_1+\frac14E_{i+1}$. So $E_2=1+\frac34E_1$ and $E_1=1+\frac34E_1+\frac14E_2$, which gives $E_1=4+E_2=4+1+\frac34E_1$, so $\frac14E_1=5$ and $E_1=20$.

**Answer: 20**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-10.title: Recurrence
hmmt-nov-2009-team-10.body:
Let $T_k$ be the expected number of doors needed, starting in room $1$, to reach room $k+1$ (room $7$ is Bowser's level). To do so Mario first reaches room $k$ (expected $T_{k-1}$ doors, with $T_0=0$), then passes one door: with probability $\frac14$ he arrives in room $k+1$, otherwise he is sent to room $1$ and must start over (expected $T_k$ more). So $T_k=T_{k-1}+1+\frac34T_k$, i.e. $T_k=4T_{k-1}+4$. This gives $T_1=4$, $T_2=20$, $T_3=84$, $T_4=340$, $T_5=1364$, $T_6=5460$.

**Answer: 5460**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-10.title: General formula
hmmt-nov-2009-team-10.body:
With $d$ doors and $r$ rooms, the same argument gives $T_k=dT_{k-1}+d$, so $T_r=d+d^2+\dots+d^r=\frac{d(d^r-1)}{d-1}$. For $d=4$, $r=6$: $\frac{4\cdot4095}{3}=5460$.

**Answer: 5460**

hmmt-nov-2009-team-11.title: Recurrence
hmmt-nov-2009-team-11.body:
Let $T_k$ be the expected number of doors needed, starting in room $1$, to reach room $k+1$ (so $T_0=0$). To get there Mario first reaches room $k$ (expected $T_{k-1}$), then passes one door: with probability $\frac1d$ he arrives in room $k+1$, otherwise (probability $\frac{d-1}d$) he is back in room $1$ and must start over. So $T_k=T_{k-1}+1+\frac{d-1}dT_k$, i.e. $T_k=dT_{k-1}+d$. Hence $T_r=d+d^2+\dots+d^r=\frac{d(d^r-1)}{d-1}$.

**Answer: $\frac{d(d^r-1)}{d-1}$**
